## Verdict on the concrete learning procedure

**Location: file page 82.** Supported, with an important qualification. The procedure is explicitly introduced as "The learning sequence proposed in Pinker (1984) was roughly as follows," and it has four steps: record the argument structures of verbs heard in the input; note whether many verbs occur in the same two argument structures and, if so, create a productive lexical rule mapping one argument structure to the other; note whether many verbs fail to occur in one form and, if the alternating verbs share a property missing in the nonalternating ones, bifurcate the classes and constrain the rule to the property-bearing class, retroactively expunging nonwitnessed forms that violate the new constraint; and, if a hypothesized constraint is falsified because many violating verbs appear in the input, search for a new distinguishing property and replace the old one.

**What is supplied versus learned.** Supplied by the input are the heard argument structures and the broad distributional patterns across the lexicon. Learned are the productive rule, the class partition, the constraining property, and any revision. The property itself is not generated from nothing: file page 82 lists the admissible kinds as a morphological or phonological property of stems, a semantic property of predicates, or a thematic property of arguments. File page 91 adds that the criteria involve concepts such as number of metrical feet, prospective possession, directness of causation, holism of filling or covering, and mapping onto a hierarchy of thematic roles.

**Is this the final settled account?** No. File page 82 presents it as a proposal from an earlier work, and file pages 91 and 92 explicitly say the criteria-based account has theoretical problems. Steven Pinker states that in the rest of the book he will show that criteria are not units the child explicitly searches for and appends to rules, but epiphenomena of more general principles of argument structure assignment, and that this yields refined criteria more likely to be exceptionless. The four-step procedure is therefore an early provisional account that later chapters are said to refine, not the book's final position.

## Verdict on the tractable candidate property inventory

**Location: file page 91.** Supported. Steven Pinker notes that the criteria are a motley collection and that the universe from which a child would sample "might be quite large." He reports that in Pinker (1984) he required the list not to be open-ended and not too large, because an open-ended list might never yield the relevant criterion and a large finite one might not be found in reasonable time. He also notes that constraints may have to be given up and searched for repeatedly, that some components such as thematic role choice and gross metrical pattern do recur across rules, but that "it is difficult to come up with an explicit list of the possible criteria." So the tractable inventory is a stated requirement of the procedure, not something the source supplies.

## Verdict on non-occurrence versus explicit negative evidence

**Location: file page 82.** Supported with a precise distinction. The procedure is sensitive to non-occurrence only in the uninteresting sense of acting differently depending on whether one hears X or does not hear X, which the text says is true of virtually any learning algorithm. It is explicitly "not sensitive to the nonoccurrence of particular sentences or even verb-argument structure combinations in parental speech"; rather it looks at broad statistical patterns across the lexicon, several layers removed from the input. No explicit correction or negative evidence is posited. File page 81 adds that scattered positive exceptions can be learned conservatively, verb by verb, from positive evidence.

## Engineering use and what remains to be invented

The source supports a reusable pattern: accumulate structured observations, induce a productive transformation when a distributional cluster warrants it, detect a partitioning property when behaviours diverge, attach the property as a gate on the transformation, retract previously generated but unwitnessed outputs when the gate is added, and replace the gate when counterexamples accumulate. This maps naturally onto executable grounded representations with a revision mechanism and a bounded hypothesis space.

What the source does not supply is the grounding itself. Argument structures are linguistic objects; nothing here tells a machine how to build representations of an external world, compose them into new ideas, preserve temporal experience, choose goals, or act. Nor does it supply the candidate property inventory, the threshold for "a large number," or the search algorithm over properties. The tractability requirement on file page 91 is an open problem the text itself flags. A machine would need to invent its own bounded, inspectable hypothesis space over grounded features, its own statistics for detecting clusters and counterexamples, and its own policy for when to generalize versus memorize.

Finally, this is a language-learning proposal. The historical criticisms of particular rule forms, such as the discussion of Fodor's objection on file page 90, concern specific linguistic rules and must not be recast as limits on all neural or connectionist implementations. Nothing here demonstrates general learning laws, and nothing here demonstrates consciousness or completed general intelligence.
